title: How a level is put together
summary: A level in R.E.P.O. is assembled rather than hand-placed: the game keeps a description of each level and then builds the map through a fixed sequence of stages before anyone is let loose in it.
body: A level starts life as a description rather than as a map. The game keeps each level as its own record with a module count, a passage limit, a note about whether it holds enemies, and a set of valuables it prefers.

That record says what the level is made from. It names normal modules, passage modules, dead ends and extraction modules alongside a number of special modules, and the generator draws on those when it lays the map out.

The build then runs in a fixed order. The game moves through its own stages: starting the level, loading, laying tiles, setting the start room, connecting objects, generating modules, blocking objects, spawning modules, marking level points, placing items and valuables, setting up and spawning players, spawning enemies, and finally finishing.

Not every level is a run. The game separates ordinary levels from run levels, the tutorial, the lobby, the main menu, the shop and recording, so the same generator ends up serving several different purposes.

A level is not one set of pieces. The modules it is made from are numbered by depth, so there is a first set of normal, passage, dead-end and extraction modules and then a second and a third, which is how a deeper run is built from different material rather than the same rooms again.

A level also has a name and a look of its own. It carries a narrative name and a translation of it, an object to connect and one to block, and its own loading graphics, so the level is presented as a place rather than as a result.

How it feels to be in is data too. Fog colour and where the fog starts and ends, an ambient colour with adaptation, colour temperature and filter, bloom, lens distortion and a vignette are all recorded per level, which is why two maps can be lit and graded differently by the same game.

The points in a level know each other. A level point records what it connects to, both the module it belongs to and the other points it joins, and the build keeps a list of all of them with a debug mesh that can be drawn when the layout is being checked.

The generator has dimensions of its own as well. It carries a width and a height, path points and a truck path, three difficulty curves and two prefabs for the player, one for the death head and one for the tumble, along with a flag for having generated and separate parents for the level and for the items it creates.
The way out is part of the map rather than a button. An extraction point is a placed thing with its own area and its own sounds, which is why escaping is something the crew has to find.
What this entry does not tell you: how large a level is, how many enemies appear, or the odds of any particular layout. We have not verified those numbers, so we do not print them.

facts.claim: A level is kept as its own description with a module count, a passage limit and a note about enemies.
That description names the kinds of module a level is built from, including normal, passage, dead-end and extraction modules.
facts.evidence: identifiers: ModulesNormal1, ModulesPassage1, ModulesDeadEnd1, ModulesExtraction1, ModulesSpecialAmount

facts.claim: A level carries a preferred set of valuables and its own start rooms.
The generator builds the level through a fixed order of stages.
The same generator serves different kinds of level, including ordinary levels, the tutorial, the shop and the lobby.
The extraction point is a placed thing with its own area.
A level's module sets are numbered by depth: after the first set there is a second and a third of the normal, passage, dead-end and extraction modules.
facts.evidence: identifiers: ModulesNormal2, ModulesNormal3, ModulesPassage2, ModulesPassage3, ModulesDeadEnd2, ModulesDeadEnd3, ModulesExtraction2, ModulesExtraction3

facts.claim: A level carries a narrative name and a localized version of it, a connect object and a block object, and its own loading graphics.
facts.evidence: identifiers: NarrativeName, NarrativeNameLocalized, ConnectObject, BlockObject, LoadingGraphic01, LoadingGraphic02, LoadingGraphic03

facts.claim: The look of a level is data as well: fog colour and its start and end distances, an ambient colour with adaptation, colour temperature and filter, bloom intensity and threshold, lens distortion, and a vignette with its own colour, intensity and smoothness.
facts.evidence: identifiers: FogColor, FogStartDistance, FogEndDistance, AmbientColor, AmbientColorAdaptation, ColorTemperature, ColorFilter, BloomIntensity, BloomThreshold, LensDistortionIntensity, VignetteColor, VignetteIntensity, VignetteSmoothness

facts.claim: The generator has a width and a height, path points and a truck path, three difficulty curves, and prefabs for the player's death head and tumble.
facts.evidence: identifiers: LevelWidth, LevelHeight, LevelPathPoints, LevelPathTruck, DifficultyCurve1, DifficultyCurve2, DifficultyCurve3, PlayerDeathHeadPrefab, PlayerTumblePrefab

facts.claim: A level point records what it connects to, both a module and the other points, and the build keeps a list of all of them with a debug mesh that can be drawn.
facts.evidence: identifiers: LevelPoint, ModuleConnect, ConnectedPoints, AllLevelPoints, DebugMeshActive, DebugMesh

facts.claim: The generator has a flag for having generated and separate parents for the level and for the items it creates.
A level is fitted out with ordinary pieces of its own as well: vent hatches, giant pipes, small lamps and oil lamps are named among them.
facts.evidence: asset names: Vent hatch Alb, Giant Pipe_DefaultMaterial_BaseColor, Small Lamp, Oil Lamp

facts.claim: A level is assembled from named modules, and one of them is kept as a template.

The shop's module family names the rooms a shop building can hold: a diner, a bunker, a car service, an upper office, an attic above the diner, a barricaded door, a big bathroom, drink machines and a painting secret shop.
facts.evidence: asset names: Module - Shop - DE - Diner, Module - Shop - DE - Bunker, Module - Shop - DE - Car Service, Module - Shop - DE - Upper Office, Module - Shop - DE - Attic above diner, Module - Shop - DE - Barricaded Door, Module - Shop - DE - Big Bathroom, Module - Shop - DE - Drink Machines, Module - Shop - DE - Painting Secret Shop

facts.claim: Stands and an extraction centre are modules of their own.
facts.evidence: asset names: Module - Shop - N - Center Extract, Module - Shop - N - Corner Stands, Module - Shop - N - Middle Stands

facts.claim: The build ships debug modules of its own, named with people's names, one of them a museum and one an outside test.
facts.evidence: asset names: Module - Debug Axel, Module - Debug Builder, Module - Debug Monika, Module - Debug Ruben - Museum, Module - Debug Ruben - outside

facts.claim: Decals are named by the surface they sit on: floor decals and ceiling decals, with a dirt decal and a set of grime decals among them.
facts.evidence: asset names: Floor Decals, Ceiling Decals, Dirt Decal, Grime Decals
